findings.summary: On October 10, 2024, FinCEN, the OCC, the Federal Reserve Board and the DOJ announced coordinated BSA/AML resolutions with TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank USA, N.A. (and parent Toronto-Dominion Bank/TD Group U.S. Holdings): FinCEN imposed a $1.3 billion civil money penalty ($757 million net after $543 million credits to DOJ/OCC), the OCC issued a cease-and-desist order with a $450 million penalty and an asset cap of ~$434 billion plus growth/business restrictions, the Federal Reserve assessed $123.5 million, and TD Bank, N.A. agreed to plead guilty to criminal violations (18 U.S.C. §371; 31 U.S.C. §§5322, 5324) with ~$1.89 billion in DOJ payments, totaling ~$3.09 billion.

On September 11, 2024, the CFPB ordered TD Bank to pay $7.76 million in redress to tens of thousands of consumers and a $20 million civil money penalty (total $28 million) for repeatedly sharing inaccurate, negative credit-card delinquency and bankruptcy information with consumer reporting companies in violation of the Fair Credit Reporting Act and Regulation V.

On August 14, 2024, the CFTC issued an order filing and settling charges against The Toronto Dominion Bank as a swap dealer for failing to maintain and preserve required records and to diligently supervise, requiring payment of a $75 million civil monetary penalty after employees including senior levels used unapproved communication methods including personal texts from at least 2015 to the present.

On August 14, 2024, the CFTC separately ordered TD Bank, as a registered swap dealer, to pay a $4 million civil monetary penalty for failing to diligently supervise its electronic communications surveillance system, resulting in failure to surveil certain communications for hundreds of swap-dealer personnel over a five-year period.

Ontario Superior Court of Justice approved settlement on February 15, 2024 in duplicative NSF fees class action against Toronto-Dominion Bank covering Canadian personal deposit account holders charged NSF fees on re-presented pre-authorized debit transactions from February 2, 2019 to November 27, 2023.

U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey gave final approval on October 15, 2024 to $32,225,000 settlement in Burns v. TD Bank, N.A. (1:21-cv-18194) alleging TD Bank improperly assessed APSN overdraft fees on transactions authorized with positive available balance but paid with insufficient funds between June 27, 2019 and September 30, 2022.

Lead plaintiffs filed Third Amended Complaint on January 31, 2025 in In re TD Bank / First Horizon Securities Litigation (D.N.J. 23-02763) on behalf of First Horizon Corporation purchasers from February 28, 2022 to May 3, 2023 alleging Toronto-Dominion Bank misrepresented Bank Secrecy Act and AML compliance causing regulators to refuse approval of its proposed acquisition of First Horizon.

Judge Renee Marie Bumb of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey dismissed on June 27, 2025 proposed class action Stevens v. TD Bank alleging TD Bank violated Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act by embedding Meta Pixel tracking code to share customers' personal financial information, finding plaintiff lacked standing but granting leave to amend.

Plaintiff filed class action on October 2, 2025 Trisal v. TD Bank, N.A. (D.N.J. 1:25-cv-16196) alleging TD Bank breached deposit agreement by assessing $35 overdraft fees on transactions cured by 11 p.m. ET next business day; federal records list case as terminated May 15, 2026.

Proposed class action filed July 8, 2026 in Ontario Superior Court of Justice by Calvin Wong against Toronto-Dominion Bank and TD Securities Inc. alleging failure to properly pay vacation and holiday pay on incentive and other pay under Employee Incentive Programs.

Judge Arun Subramanian of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York partially denied on October 13, 2026 defendants' motion to dismiss securities fraud class action Tiessen v. Toronto-Dominion Bank (24-cv-8032) alleging misrepresentations that TD was committed to AML controls while senior management knew of long-term systemic deficiencies; case proceeding to discovery.

Ontario Superior Court Justice Janet Leiper granted leave and certified on November 3, 2026 misrepresentation class action against Toronto-Dominion Bank and senior leaders including former CEO Bharat Masrani alleging TD misrepresented AML control deficiencies from 2021-2024 while its U.S. subsidiaries became first U.S. banks to plead guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering and U.S. regulators imposed US$3.09 billion in penalties; suit claims CA$30 billion market capitalization loss.

TD Bank N.A. and its parent TD Bank US Holding Company pleaded guilty on Oct. 10, 2024 to conspiring to fail to maintain an AML program compliant with the Bank Secrecy Act, fail to file accurate Currency Transaction Reports, and launder monetary instruments for failures from Jan. 2014-Oct. 2023 that left 92% of transaction volume (~$18.3 trillion) unmonitored and enabled three money laundering networks to move >$670 million through TD Bank accounts, including >$400 million for Da Ying Sze; DOJ imposed $1.8 billion penalty and FinCEN $1.3 billion as part of almost $3.1 billion coordinated resolution requiring overhaul, independent monitor and cooperation.

TD Bank assistant store manager Wilfredo Aquino pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder monetary instruments for leveraging his position from 2019-Feb. 2021 to facilitate Da Ying Sze's network moving ~$474 million through TD Bank accounts via cash deposits in New York/New Jersey, accepting >$11,000 in retail gift cards as bribes.

TD Bank employee Nunez of Scotch Plains, NJ pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and receipt of bribes by a bank employee for accepting bribes from March 2021-Oct. 2023 to open dozens of shell-company accounts and issue ~600 debit cards used for >120,000 ATM withdrawals in Colombia to expatriate >$26 million.

Former TD Bank employee Leonardo Ayala pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and receipt of bribes by a bank employee for opening fraudulent accounts and issuing >150 debit cards from June-Nov. 2023 used for >12,000 ATM withdrawals in Colombia funneling ~$5.5 million in exchange for >$6,000 in bribes.

Former TD Bank employee Gerardo Aquino pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and receipt of bribes by a bank employee for accepting bribes and abusing his position at TD Bank to launder >$4.8 million to Colombia.

On December 23, 2021 OFAC announced a $115,005.04 settlement with T.D. Bank, N.A. for apparent violations of the North Korea Sanctions Regulations (processing 1,479 transactions totaling $382,685.38 and maintaining nine accounts for employees of the North Korean mission to the United Nations without a license) and the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations (maintaining accounts and enabling 145 transactions totaling $35,514.13 for a U.S. resident on the SDN List).

NCB Management Services, a TD Bank vendor, suffered a breach beginning February 1, 2023 via a misconfigured database, exposing over 1 million records including TD Bank customers' names, addresses, SSNs, account numbers and credit card details later listed on the dark web; TD Bank filed notice with the Maine Attorney General and class action lawsuits followed.

Former TD Bank employee gained unauthorized access to customer information between August and December 2022, disclosed to Massachusetts regulators in February 2025, exposing names, SSNs, dates of birth, addresses, government-issued IDs, Social Security cards, pay stubs, W-2 forms and financial account and credit/debit card numbers; TD Bank terminated the employee and investigated with law enforcement.

TD Bank insider incident between January 7-30, 2026 where an employee accessed customer records without authorization, reported June 15, 2026 to regulators, compromising names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, SSNs, account numbers and transactional data; bank offered identity protection and a class action alleging negligence is progressing.

TD Bank disclosed September 15, 2026 to the Massachusetts Office of Consumer Affairs and Business Regulation a new data security event that may have resulted in unauthorized access/disclosure of personal and financial information including names, SSNs, dates of birth, addresses, government-issued IDs, pay stubs, W-2s, financial account and credit/debit card numbers, affecting 54 Massachusetts residents (nationwide total undisclosed); bank offered 2-year Fraud-Defender monitoring and to cover account replacement costs.

Between January 2014 and October 2023 TD Bank leadership knowingly presided over a criminally deficient anti-money laundering program used to launder money for fentanyl and human trafficking rings, with high-level executives including the person who became chief anti-money laundering officer aware of serious problems but failing to correct them, resulting in a historic $3 billion fine, plea agreement and consent order; sources allege senior management repeatedly ignored internal warning calls and whistleblowers who tried to fix problems internally before going to the government, while DOJ charged only two low-level employees.

CFPB ordered TD Bank to pay $28 million after finding management prioritized growth over compliance, repeatedly furnishing inaccurate and suspected fraudulent account information to consumer reporting companies, knowing of systemic errors for more than a year before fixing them and failing to conduct proper investigations of disputes, affecting hundreds of thousands of customers.
